tweets.text:
Protecting enterprise data in a world where agents are using our systems 100X more than people ever did is going to be one of the more complex security and governance challenges of the 21st century. 

Importantly, security and productivity gains are inexorably linked in the world of AI. If you give an agent too much unfettered information access, it will be difficult to truly control and protect your data; and conversely, if you lock everything down completely, you won’t get any real productivity gains from AI.

We need all new ways to protect our systems, environments, and structured and unstructured dada in the enterprise in an intelligent way by modernizing our approach to security and governance.

At Box, as one example, we’re building new intelligent ways to protect enterprise data and agentic use of that information. A recent update in Box Shield is to provide granular controls on what content agents can and can’t work with based on document classification level. We’re also working on other features that can automatically detect and alert (or block) when data is being accessed or used in unusual or anomalous ways by agents.

And this is just the start. There’s a ton more innovation coming across the entire industry - from the labs like OpenAI or Anthropic; security platforms like Palo Alto Networks, Cisco, CrowdStrike, Okta; or startups like Enclave, Method, Alterion, Runlayer, and many many others - to rethink how we protect information in the world of AI agents. Exciting and wild times ahead.

tweets.text:
I have been obsessed with closed payment loops for a LONG time, and have been looking to find a company trying to solve a real problem.. excited to finally back Piston (piston dot com) ⛽️

USA alone spends hundreds of billions in fuel. Most of that spend comes through cards (credit, fuel, or sometime house cards). However, a lot of these cards are not even tied to a particular driver. They often get stolen, skimmed, or misused. The fleet owner then has to eat the fraud and then spend a long time reconciling what exactly happened. The gas station has to pay interchange fees to accept the card, but has no relationship with the fleets on the other side. And a lot of companies have come and gone trying to optimize this infrastructure rather than thinking about it from the very beginning.

You really can't fix this issue by JUST building a better fuel card. The card is the problem, and so Piston decided to get rid of it. It moves the payment over its own rails without networks or any intermediaries. Piston pays the station and then invoices the fleet. Every transaction is tied to a specific driver with the time, location, and fuel type attached, and soon it'll be integrated with the vehicle itself.

The founders faced this problem themselves. @vik_sekhon runs his own fleet of trucks, and his fleet lost real money to fuel fraud. @Shivam2291 used to recruit thousands of drivers before the two of them got together to help build Piston. The best signal for how effective Piston is for fleets is the moment they switch over to Piston, they see their fuel spend automatically go down. I have seen so many charts and customer quotes that show this directly.

Customer love shows in the metrics. Payment volume has grown 8x and merchant network has grown 40x while retention has stayed above 98%. Piston is now live across 2,000 stations and across 48 states. Fleets pay nothing for it today and they get fraud prevention, which is what a card-based system cannot offer. Gas stations get direct access to fleets to help build loyalty and offer adjacent products.

To increase their reach, Piston is now directly integrated with POS of the majority of gas stations in America. This allows them to turn on hundreds of gas stations at once, secure supply and hence fulfill their already burgeoning demand. 

Thrilled to be leading their Series A and joining the board, along with existing investors @sparkcapital & @pearvc. Special thanks to @arpans who introduced me to this team last year!

Protecting enterprise data in a world where agents are using our systems 100X more than people ever did is going to be one of the more complex security and governance challenges of the 21st century.

If you give an agent too much unfettered information access, it will be difficult to truly control and protect your data; and conversely, if you lock everything down completely, you won’t get any real productivity gains from AI.

We need all new ways to protect our systems, environments, and structured and unstructured dada in the enterprise in an intelligent way by modernizing our approach to security and governance.

I have been obsessed with closed payment loops for a LONG time, and have been looking to find a company trying to solve a real problem.. excited to finally back Piston (piston dot com) ⛽️

USA alone spends hundreds of billions in fuel. Most of that spend comes through cards (credit, fuel, or sometime house cards). However, a lot of these cards are not even tied to a particular driver. They often get stolen, skimmed, or misused. The fleet owner then has to eat the fraud and then spend a long time reconciling what exactly happened. The gas station has to pay interchange fees to accept the card, but has no relationship with the fleets on the other side. And a lot of companies have come and gone trying to optimize this infrastructure rather than thinking about it from the very beginning.

You really can't fix this issue by JUST building a better fuel card. The card is the problem, and so Piston decided to get rid of it. It moves the payment over its own rails without networks or any intermediaries. Piston pays the station and then invoices the fleet. Every transaction is tied to a specific driver with the time, location, and fuel type attached, and soon it'll be integrated with the vehicle itself.

The founders faced this problem themselves. @vik_sekhon runs his own fleet of trucks, and his fleet lost real money to fuel fraud. @Shivam2291 used to recruit thousands of drivers before the two of them got together to help build Piston. The best signal for how effective Piston is for fleets is the moment they switch over to Piston, they see their fuel spend automatically go down. I have seen so many charts and customer quotes that show this directly.

Customer love shows in the metrics. Payment volume has grown 8x and merchant network has grown 40x while retention has stayed above 98%. Piston is now live across 2,000 stations and across 48 states. Fleets pay nothing for it today and they get fraud prevention, which is what a card-based system cannot offer. Gas stations get direct access to fleets to help build loyalty and offer adjacent products.

To increase their reach, Piston is now directly integrated with POS of the majority of gas stations in America. This allows them to turn on hundreds of gas stations at once, secure supply and hence fulfill their already burgeoning demand.

tweets.text:
There are two ways AI progress could go very badly and that we must avoid.

First, we could lose control of the future to AI. This is unacceptable; we are unapologetically on Team Humanity, and AI must always serve people. To ensure that, we need ways to ensure that alignment and safety techniques stay ahead of progress in model capabilities.

Second, we could end up in a world with too much concentration of power. If an extraordinarily powerful AI is used by one person or company to impress their worldview onto everyone else, the results could be extremely dystopian.

Avoiding these two threats requires walking a narrow middle path; for example, one country could gain too much power. Another example is one lab ending up with too much power.
tweets.summary_zh:
AI的发展有两个主要的潜在风险，我们必须避免。

首先，我们可能会失去对AI的控制，这样未来就不受我们掌握了。这是不行的，我们始终站在“人类”的一方，AI必须为人类服务。为了确保这一点，我们需要在AI技术进步的同时，强化安全和对齐的措施。

第二个风险是权力过于集中。如果一个特别强大的AI被某个人或公司用来影响大家的想法，结果可能会非常糟糕。

The world deserves confidence that American companies developing increasingly capable AI will act responsibly, especially as the trajectory of progress has steepened. Every frontier lab must deliver on this, and there is no reason any of us should come to work if we cannot.

We welcome a federal framework that sets consistent safety requirements for frontier AI. But we do not believe we need to wait for an anti-trust exemption or legislation to begin the work of providing this confidence. Consistent rules to manage frontier risk so that we can maximize the benefits are a good idea (and we are excited by ideas like independent auditors).

Years ago, companies like ours developed things like Responsible Scaling Policies and Preparedness Frameworks. Those were good for that moment, and focused primarily on the deployment of completed models, not what happens during their development process.

Today's shift to focusing on safe development and evaluation will need new tools. For example, at OpenAI we now formulate explicit safety cases in advance of frontier reinforcement learning runs we expect to significantly increase capability, in addition to the safety work we have long done in advance of model releases.

We hope that other companies will learn from our approaches and propose their own; we think shared standards for misalignment, monitoring, and safety will lead to better outcomes. We look forward to collaborating with our colleagues across the industry to formulate the best version of these.

When we talk about “pacing”, we do not mean “stopping”. Progress has been rapid and will continue to be. But it should be slower than it otherwise could be; interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs.

Pacing will be well worth this cost; no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness, or let capabilities get ahead of alignment and monitoring.

Where we will need the help of our government is for international coordination. But first we should do what we can ourselves.

The team structure, product patterns, how you launch and learn that got you here do not work with AI. Much of product development over the last 15 yrs has been incremental improvements.

AI requires experimentation and invention.

2/ Under-investing in evals

Most enterprises don't quite understand the importance of this and what good looks like here. (I have a whole evals series in the comments - check it out)

3/ Building AI for the company from the outside

The central AI team declares itself a platform team and builds tools that everyone is supposed to adopt.

These products are often disconnected from the actual workflows, context and judgment of the people doing the work.

Begrudging adoption follows. But not meaningful productivity gains.

What you should do:

1/ Hire leaders who have done successfully built AI products. You need technical/product depth plus the ability to earn trust with the people whose jobs they’re helping reinvent.

2/ Make evals a first class citizen in your AI efforts

3/ Embed your best AI builders inside the functions you want to transform. Build * with * finance , build * with * sales, build * with * support.

tweets.text:
My 9/11 story
(lightly updated version of a blog post I wrote in 2016 for the 15th anniversary)

In September 2001, I was the young co-founder of a NYC tech startup, TripleHop Technologies.   

We were building enterprise search software, using whatever AI existed at the time, building what would be today close to what a Glean does.  

We had maybe 25 people on the team at the time.  Pretty much all of us were at the very begining of our careers, barely out of school, unexperienced, but highly enthusiastic.

Our office was located on the 53rd floor of the North Tower at the World Trade Center.

We had ended up at the World Trade Center fairly randomly.  Our first office was located on Water Street, right above a 24 hour McDonald’s.  It looked more like a decrepit apartment than an actual office, occasionally didn’t smell that great, but it was cheap and good enough.

But after a year or so, the team had grown, and that office had become too small, so we started looking for a bigger one.

At the time, for a reason or another, there wasn’t a lot of office inventory on the market in the area where we wanted to be.  

We looked for a bit, couldn’t find anything suitable, until one of us had the strange idea of inquiring at the World Trade Center, which felt like a long shot. 

Turned out that the World Trade Center had some smaller offices, and some availability.  In those dot-com bubble days, they also were quite eager to attract young tech startups, and were willing to offer us some preferential terms. 

So we went to take a look, and visited two offices in the North Tower. 

One was a large office at the very top of the building, perhaps the 104th floor, I don’t exactly recall. It had unbelievable views, but it really felt like taking that office would be pushing it – even with a good deal, we were just a little seed-funded startup, after all. Also, the elevator ride took forever. 

So instead we chose the smaller, cheaper office on the 53rd floor.  

We really liked our new office, and the World Trade Center in general.  It felt like a little town, with a lot of retail and amenities below the surface, and its own subway station. We ate a bit too often at a Sbarro joint located right outside the ground floor elevator.

The night before 9/11, my co-founder Renaud Laplanche and I worked very late into the evening, as we did most nights.  In true nerdy founder fashion, we played a ping pong game or two, as we did pretty much every time before calling it a night – the ping pong table being our attempt at creating a startup culture.  

I left, and think Renaud may have stayed on that night to finish working on a proposal for a prospective customer.

The morning after, when the plane hit the North Tower at 8:46am, I was home, about to leave for work.   

Like many young tech people, we were night owls but not early birds, typically showing up at the office around 9:30am.  

I had the TV on, and as about to turn it off and walk out of the door, saw the “breaking news” scroll at the bottom of the screen mentioning a plane collision, but no image.    

As I had a faraway view of the World Trade Center from the window of my West Village studio apartment, I looked up and saw what seemed like a little bit of smoke at the top.

I assumed the plane that had hit the tower was a small tourist plane.  We would often see them fly by the office, above the nearby Hudson River, often at altitudes that felt very close to us.  It had crossed my mind more than once that it wouldn’t take that much for one of them to hit the tower by accident.

Then, like so many others, I saw those unbelievable images on TV. I called my family back in France.  Shortly thereafter, phone lines went down. 

The rest of the day was surreal and gut-wrenching, although I remember feeling mostly numb.

I went on a mad scramble to see if everyone at TripleHop was ok. For many hours, we just didn’t know.  With no phone working, we accounted for most people via email, but a number did not reply for a while.

It eventually turned out only one person from the team, Kenton Beerman, was at the office at 8:46am.   He made it out shocked but unscathed.

Perhaps as a way to cope psychologically, or just because they were amazing people, I remember that the team was incredibly focused on saving the business that day.  

This was obviously pre-AWS, we had our own server room in our office, but thankfully our CTO Joaquin Delgado and his team had backed everything up.  By the end of the day, we were essentially back up and running.

After a few days, we found shared office space.  But business didn’t go back to usual. In addition to everything else, 9/11 was the final nail in the coffin for the economy after the dot com bubble burst.  The next couple of years were a complete nuclear winter.

Thankfully, we had raised a $5M Series A (a solid amount at hte time!) a few months before 9/11, which kept us afloat.  We also managed to win a few deals in Europe, which gave us a bit more cash.  

Eventually business picked up strongly in late 2003 and 2004, potential acquirers came knocking, and TripleHop was acquired by Oracle in 2005.

We all went on with our lives.  My co-founder Renaud reached extraordinary entrepreneurial success and defined a whole new industry.

We all have families now.  I occasionally see pictures of beautiful children on my Facebook feed.  

I rarely talk about 9/11, and have tried to not think about it too much. 

It took me a very long time to go visit the 9/11 memorial downtown.  

I finally made it just a few weeks ago, after a board meeting nearby, walking there almost by accident.

Looking at the names engraved in the marble, I was reminded that it wouldn’t have taken much.  An hour later, a few floors lower. Or choosing that office on the 104th floor instead of the other one, a few months prior.

And I feel deeply connected not just to those names, but to New York. 

Before 9/11, New York felt like an exciting, but ultimately foreign, city. After 9/11, I truly started feeling like a New Yorker.  

Everyone remembers where they were on 9/11.  Everyone has a story of some sort, many infinitely more tragic.  

This is just mine.

Hey ████,

I think there is room for both.

1. Prototypes and other throw-away code can be treated as totally black box. If you’re going to throw it away anyway, and if the blast radius of it breaking is low, it doesn’t need to be perfect.
2. Production code written by Claude should have a higher bar than if it was written by a human. At Anthropic, we have many guardrails in place to make sure this is happening: lots of lint rules, lots of tests, Claude-driven end to end tests, Claude-powered fuzzers running daily, automated code reviews and security reviews, automated code refactoring, and so on. Without these, you can end up with a mess that is hard to maintain down the line. Luckily, the model makes it increasingly easy to do these well — run a few daily routines, use Claude Code Review, etc.

Your job is to hold the bar on code quality. If Claude’s code doesn’t meet the bar, try:
- Using the latest frontier model (Opus 5 or Fable 5.1)
- Increase effort to high or xhigh
- Invest in your CLAUDE.md and skills to succinctly teach Claude how to work in your codebase

If all else fails, steer Claude more when you work with it, or have Claude fix accumulated debt and rewrite your codebase to make it easier to work with. Or, wait for the next model.

Best,

tweets.text:
How to build great evals - part 10

Measure the steps, not just the result.

Much like high school math, it isn’t sufficient just to get the right answer, the steps to get there are critical.

Two agent trajectories might produce the same answer (42!!).

but one of them  searches the right sources, retrieves the right document, makes 4 clean tool calls and calculates the result. The other makes 17 calls, searches the same thing 3 times, recovers from 2 errors and eventually gets there. 

It’s clear which one is better.

Here’s what you need to do:
1/ clearly define your whole workflow
2/ define the tasks in each step
3/ think through how you measure each step - separate evals or is it a slice of a bigger eval
4/ define your median and hard tasks - reflect them in your evals

Now any time you look at eval results, study the steps first and the final results next.
tweets.summary_zh:
要打造优秀的评估系统，不能只关注最终结果，还得重视整个过程。就像高中数学，单靠答案不够，解决问题的步骤同样重要。有的AI做同样的工作，但用的步骤和方法不同，效率和效果也会有差距。

你需要做的：
1. 明确整个工作流程；
2. 定义每一步的任务；
3. 考虑如何衡量每一步的表现，是分别评估还是作为更大评估的一部分；
4. 确定中等和难度任务，并在评估中反映出来。

所以，下次看评估结果时，先看过程，再看最终结果哦！

tweets.text:
Some more tales from the road. Met with a couple dozen technology leaders this week across banking, media, information services, insurance, and consulting to discuss agents in the enterprise.

Some of the biggest trends right now:

* Cyber! Everyone nervous about the growing rate of vulnerabilities coming at them from AI, and the implications of the OpenAI Hugging Face incident. The conversation is not as existential as it is in Silicon Valley, but still highly concerned and pragmatic about what to do about it operationally in their environments. Lots of new discoveries due to AI, and still hard to keep up with all the changes they have to execute now.

* Model battles persist. Most companies are deploying multiple frontier models within their enterprise. Too hard to standardize on anything and seeing different preferences across their teams and use cases. But the dollars are still concentrated on just a few vendors. Open weights still in infancy at scale in most of these organizations, often due to lack of domestic “frontier” OSS options. Plenty of appetite for more options here, but so far few places to go.

* Agent security and identity. Somewhat tied to Hugging Face, there’s much more awareness to the new challenges around agent security and identity management in a world when agents are trying to get into every system they can. In a perfect world enterprises could setup identities for all their agents and control what they’re doing, but of course sometimes the agent needs to act exactly as the user as well.

* Process reengineering. Most companies realizing that the big upside of agents is when they can change the actual workflow itself to get the full gains from AI. Far more ROI when companies can adjust their workflows to support agents changing how the work happens instead of just layering on agents into the existing flow. But the big question is who can actually tackle driving these changes, where does that live, etc. Best lessons were still around embedded FDEs in the functions.

* Ruthless adjusting of architectures. Most companies had examples of changing systems out multiple times just in the past year or two with different vendors. I probably haven’t heard “we tried X and it didn’t work so have gone with Y” more than in today’s environment. The lesson here is that because innovation is happening so fast, no one hangs around until a vendor gets something right, they just move on to the next one. 

* Evals! Still very early for most companies to have a good grasp of evals of their workflows. A few customers out of a couple dozen called this out - huge opportunity right now for enterprises to have a good sense of how their work actually happens and how well AI is doing against it.

* Legacy systems still a hurdle. As always, legacy systems still remain a mainstay issue that holds back enterprises from rapid adoption of AI in enterprises. Data is fragmented across legacy environments that weren’t built for an agentic world. Companies spending a lot of time just cleaning up these old platforms. 

Many more topics, but these tend to be some of the more top of mind items at the moment in the enterprise.

tweets.text:
The way to the reconcile capability level of AI vs. GDP impact is that the diffusion of AI will take much longer than people think. And it will also show up in ways that are hard to measure in GDP immediately. 

You could bring the world’s greatest superintelligence to many workflows, and still be bound by the laws of corporate physics: getting data prepared and put into a pipeline, process reengineering and change management, aligning on how the new workflow should function, and so on.

Even after you solve all that, you’re still bound by the speed of the real world: waiting for a customer to respond to a proposal, getting a permit for a project, a drug discovery pipeline taking years to eventually reach the consumer, and so on. Not to mention lots of positive daily AI use-cases are entirely net neutral to GDP, at least in the near term.

AI diffusion is going to be the theme of the next decade. The upside is that there’s a tremendous amount of opportunity in building the bridges between superintelligence and real-world workflows.

tweets.text:
this is a very good and well designed report

however, two impt assumptions in it that significantly change the analysis once you start to play with it:

1. the report assumes that jobs can be decomposed into tasks
2. the report models human tasks created by automation always as a fraction of automated tasks. in other words, the underlying assumptions is automation always reduces human labor (or at best leaves it the same)

taken in reverse order:

does automation always reduce human work?
in my experience, the answer is no. automation often creates multiples more work for humans. 

i have a full argument here (https://t.co/Lb7SUCe2pO) for why this is structurally true. but i think any honest analysis of the economic impacts of AI has to take work creation seriously. 

can jobs be decomposed into tasks?
yes, that is a useful lens. but lists of tasks is a way of looking at jobs—one that makes the question of how much of a job is automatable actually tractable. therefore, it's useful.

but this is not the full picture, it's just jobs as exposed to our method of questioning. 

a good example: under this model, where do the new tasks come from? are they just from bosses that add a list to the task list for workers to complete? where do those tasks come from? unless you can model that well you are missing a key term in the analysis (see the first point above.)

another way of looking at this, borrowing from wittgenstein and heidegger, is that a job is a particular way of seeing and caring about the world. an editor notices things a nurse doesn’t, and vice versa. what you care about shapes what you notice, what seems worth doing, and what counts as doing it well. you can make some of that explicit as a task list. but as your tools and circumstances change, the same cares can generate entirely new tasks. that process is part of the job.

the above is completely missing from this analysis (understandably because it's, by definition, very hard to model!) 

but if you take it seriously, it shoudl substantially change your perspective automation and jobs
tweets.summary_zh:
这份报告设计得很好，但有两个假设会影响结论。首先，它认为工作可以分解成任务；其次，它假设自动化总是会减少人类的工作量。实际上，自动化常常会带来更多的工作。

工作虽然可以分解成任务，但这只是理解工作的一个角度，而不是完整的看法。新任务的来源和任务变化的过程也非常重要，但这些在报告中没有考虑到。如果认真对待这些问题，自动化和工作之间的关系可能会有很大的不同。

On the one hand, who doesn’t want a personalized vaccine that treats their cancer and reduces the need for chemo?

On the other hand, there are many patients and families desperately looking for treatment. 

Presenting this as what cancer treatment looks like in 2026 is just not true:

2. A treatment showing promise in a trial doesn’t mean most patients can get it or benefit from it.

Good reminder here that with rapidly accelerating AI progress, you should likely be building with a vision that contemplates at least a few orders of magnitude of capability improvement or token volume available to you.

The best opportunities right now are those where you can value to customers today with things that are barely only possible, but with a full mission that feels nearly impossible with today’s tech.

tweets.text:
The AI jobs prediction so far is playing out the opposite of what many thought.

The reason this is happening is because AI is bringing automation to areas that don’t have finite demand characteristics. AI allows companies to do far more than they could before, but agents still require human operators and oversight to generate value from them. 

And not only has AI not replaced many of the types of jobs that theoretically would have been most affected by AI - engineers or lawyers - but AI is also creating or growing entire categories of jobs across the economy. 

Cybersecurity, FDEs, agent operators, engineers in non-software domains, and tons of job categories are going to explode. It’s not clear if or when this trend will reverse because we keep discovering all new areas of demand that AI is going to open up.

podcasts.title: How agents are perfect for Linux | DHH and Lex Fridman
podcasts.summary_zh:
在这个视频中，DHH 和 Lex Fridman 探讨了 Linux 操作系统的优势以及如何通过智能代理提升用户体验。他们讨论了代理在操作系统中的重要性，以及它们如何增强工作效率和创意设计流程。

💡 值得一看 — 视频中的讨论涉及操作系统与智能代理的结合，可能对 Logic Labs 和 TexTale 在技术应用和创意设计方面提供启发。

podcasts.title: GG Navier Stokes, Math Wars, Greg Brockman Joins, Scott Wu Joins, The Seufenator Joins

这个视频讨论了Navier-Stokes方程在数学领域的争议，以及Greg Brockman和Scott Wu等人在AI界的重要动态。视频涵盖了当前AI行业的趋势和发展，尤其关注与复杂数学问题和算法相关的挑战。

💡 值得一看 — 该视频可以帮助你了解AI领域的最新发展和技术挑战，这对Logic Labs和TexTale在电商和创意设计中的应用自有启发。

producthunt.name: Clipto MCP
producthunt.tagline: Let agents source clips from terabytes of your local video
producthunt.summary_zh: Clipto MCP 是一款视频剪辑工具，允许用户从本地海量视频中快速提取片段。它支持高效整理和查找视频素材，方便用户在创作中使用。

producthunt.name: Astute
producthunt.tagline: Automate your B2B brand going viral, with new media creators
producthunt.summary_zh: Astute 是一个自动化平台，帮助企业与新媒体创作者合作，快速提升品牌知名度。通过简化品牌宣传流程，企业可以轻松实现内容的病毒式传播。

producthunt.name: Kilo Code for JetBrains
producthunt.tagline: Fully native, open-source coding agent built for JetBrains
producthunt.summary_zh: Kilo Code for JetBrains 是一款完全原生的开源编码助手，专为 JetBrains 开发环境设计。它能够提高编码效率，提供智能代码建议和自动完成功能，让开发者更轻松地编写程序。

producthunt.name: Meridian
producthunt.tagline: Don't let your work go unnoticed. Get promoted!
producthunt.summary_zh: Meridian是一款专注于职业发展的工具。它可以帮助用户记录并展示自己的工作成就，让你在职场上获得更多关注和晋升机会。通过使用Meridian，你可以轻松整理和分享自己的工作亮点。

producthunt.name: Mastra Factory
producthunt.tagline: From issue to production, run by agents.
producthunt.summary_zh: Mastra Factory 是一个自动化平台，专为管理生产流程而设计。用户可以通过平台提交问题，从而直接将其转化为生产任务，整个过程由代理人进行协调与执行。简而言之，它简化了产品从问题到生产的转化流程。

producthunt.name: Switch
producthunt.tagline: Bring any AI agent into Slack, Teams & Discord
producthunt.summary_zh: Switch是一款可以将各种AI助手集成到Slack、Teams和Discord中的工具。用户可以通过这个平台轻松接入不同的AI代理，以提高团队的沟通和协作效率。它简化了工作流程，让员工能够快速获取所需的信息和支持。

producthunt.name: x1
producthunt.tagline: Lovable for iPhone apps go from idea to App Store
producthunt.summary_zh: x1 是一个帮助用户将想法转化为 iPhone 应用的工具。它提供从概念设计到提交 App Store 的完整流程，用户可以轻松创建和发布自己的应用程序。

producthunt.name: GPT-6 Astra
producthunt.tagline: OpenAI's most capable model for end-to-end work
producthunt.summary_zh: GPT-6 Astra 是 OpenAI 最新的人工智能模型，具备强大的自然语言处理能力。它可以完成从文本生成到对话理解等多种任务，适用于自动化工作和内容创作。

producthunt.name: Monid
producthunt.summary_zh: Monid是一个为代理工具提供支持的开放式路由平台。它可以帮助用户快速集成和管理不同的代理工具，提升工作效率。用户可以通过Monid轻松连接和使用各种应用程序。

producthunt.name: Anysite.io
producthunt.tagline: Build and enrich B2B lists by chatting to your agent
producthunt.summary_zh: Anysite.io 是一个可以让用户通过聊天与智能助手互动的平台，用于创建和丰富B2B（企业对企业）的潜在客户名单。用户只需与助手对话，就能快速获取和整理所需的商业信息。这个工具简化了数据收集过程，提高了工作效率。

producthunt.name: PaymentKit
producthunt.tagline: Billing that survives a processor shutdown
producthunt.summary_zh: PaymentKit是一款支付处理工具，能够在支付处理器出现故障时继续进行账单和交易。它确保用户的付款流程不会中断，提高了支付的可靠性和效率。

producthunt.name: Naoma AI Demo Agent V2
producthunt.tagline: Turns website traffic into booked, qualified meetings
producthunt.summary_zh: Naoma AI Demo Agent V2是一款智能工具，能够将网站访问者转化为预约的合格会议。它利用人工智能分析访客行为，提高转化率，简化预约流程。通过这款产品，企业可以更有效地管理潜在客户互动。

producthunt.name: Clara AI SDR
producthunt.tagline: Turn website visitors into qualified pipeline
producthunt.summary_zh: Clara AI SDR 是一款自动化的软件工具，可以将访问网站的访客转化为潜在客户。通过智能分析和交互，它能够识别有意向的访客并收集相关信息，帮助企业建立更高效的客户销售漏斗。

producthunt.name: AI Toolbox 3.0
producthunt.tagline: Search, organize and export every AI chat in one place
producthunt.summary_zh: AI Toolbox 3.0 是一款集中管理AI聊天记录的工具。用户可以在一个地方搜索、整理并导出所有的AI对话，方便快速查找和使用信息。该产品让AI聊天记录的管理变得简单高效。

producthunt.name: Widgo
producthunt.tagline: AI Sales rep for your website visitors
producthunt.summary_zh: Widgo是一款网站访客的AI销售助手，它能通过智能对话与潜在客户互动，回答问题并提供产品信息。这个工具可以帮助提高转化率，简化客户咨询流程。

github_trending.description: Run frontier MoE models on hardware you already own — pure C, zero deps, experts streamed from disk. Tiny engine, immense model. 🐦
github_trending.summary_zh:
这个项目是一个轻量级的工具，可以让用户在自己已有的硬件上运行大型的AI模型，而不需要繁琐的依赖配置。 

对于Yves来说，这个项目主要可以帮助Logic Labs（AI公司）在无需额外投资硬件的情况下，优化AI模型的运行效率，从而推动AI技术的发展与应用。作为创意设计从业者，他也能利用这种工具探索更高效的AI模型来提升设计创意的实现速度。

github_trending.description: Fast, efficient, battle-tested at Alibaba's scale. Hybrid architecture code review tool: deterministic pipelines + LLM Agent, precise line-level comments, built-in multi-language ruleset (NPE, thread-safety, XSS, SQL injection), OpenAI & Anthropic compatible.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个代码审查工具，可以快速、高效地检查代码中的错误，确保软件安全和质量，同时支持多种编程语言。对Yves的Logic Labs（AI公司）会有更直接的帮助，因为它可以提升软件开发的质量和速度，从而加速AI工具的迭代与应用，对他作为创意设计从业者的工作效率也会有积极的促进作用。

github_trending.description: YuE2: frontier music generation with symbolic planning, zero-shot covers, and agentic music editing.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目 YuE2 旨在利用人工智能进行音乐创作，包括生成音乐、创作音乐封面和编辑音轨，让用户在没有音乐专业知识的情况下也能创作出高质量的音乐作品。对于 Yves 来说，这个项目可以为 Logic Labs 提供新的音乐生成技术，进而为其 AI 产品增添更丰富的创意表现，另外也可以为 TexTale 的电商平台提供更具吸引力的音乐内容，提升用户体验。

github_trending.description: VoiceStudio is the open-source, fully-local ElevenLabs alternative — voice cloning, voice design, video dubbing, dictation, transcription & audiobook creation in 646 languages.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这项目是一个开源工具，可以让用户创建和克隆自己的声音，进行视频配音、文字转语音、听书等功能，支持多达646种语言。对Yves的Logic Labs（AI公司）有帮助，因为可以利用这个技术为AI应用开发更丰富的语音交互功能，同时也能为TexTale（科技服装电商）提供更个性化的客户服务体验，增强品牌的用户参与感。作为创意设计从业者，这个工具可以为Yves的创意项目提供更多声音设计的可能性，有助于提升作品的表现力。

github_trending.description: A Simple and Universal Swarm Intelligence Engine, Predicting Anything. 简洁通用的群体智能引擎，预测万物
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个简单且通用的群体智能引擎，可以用来预测各种事物的趋势和变化，利用群体智慧的力量解决问题。对Yves来说，这个项目可以为Logic Labs提供强大的数据分析和预测能力，帮助其在AI领域更好地理解市场动态和用户需求，同时也可以为TexTale在电商战略和产品设计上提供数据驱动的洞察。作为创意设计从业者，Yves还可以利用该工具进行创意预测，提升设计决策的科学性。

github_trending.description: Give your AI agent eyes to see the entire internet. Read & search Twitter, Reddit, YouTube, GitHub, Bilibili, XiaoHongShu — one CLI, zero API fees.
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目可以让你的 AI 代理在网络上进行搜索和阅读，包括 Twitter、Reddit、YouTube 等多个平台，用户只需要使用一个命令行工具，完全不需要支付 API 费用。对 Yves 来说，这对 Logic Labs (AI 公司) 特别有帮助，因为它可以提升 AI 项目的信息获取能力，从而更好地分析行业趋势和数据支持创意设计。

github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目收集了多种人工智能系统的提示信息，帮助用户理解和利用这些先进模型的功能。对Yves而言，这个项目在Logic Labs（AI 公司）中可能特别有帮助，因为他可以利用这些提示优化AI应用的设计和功能，从而提升产品的创新性和用户体验。同时，对于TexTale（科技服装电商），了解AI的系统提示也能在品牌营销和客户沟通中提供提升。

github_trending.description: All in one plugin for Hermes Agent ⚚ the coding intelligence, a long-term memory system and model optimized workflow packages
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个集成插件，旨在增强 Hermes Agent 的智能编程能力，提供长期记忆系统和优化工作流程的工具包。对于 Yves 来说，这个项目可以在 Logic Labs（AI 公司）中帮助提升 AI 相关产品的开发效率，同时也可能为 TexTale 在技术灵活性和创新设计方面提供支持，使得他能够更好地运用 AI 工具进行创作。

github_trending.description: An open-source cross-platform alternative to AirDrop
github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个开源的跨平台文件传输工具，类似于 Apple 的 AirDrop，允许用户在设备之间快速分享文件，而无需互联网连接。对Yves的TexTale科技服装电商业务有帮助，可以在产品拍摄、设计反馈等场景中，快速与团队成员或合作伙伴分享视觉素材和设计文件，提高工作效率。同时，作为创意设计从业者，LocaSend 提供的便捷文件传输功能，能够支持他更有效地进行创作和设计协作。

github_trending.summary_zh: 这个项目是一个与 Bitwarden 兼容的密码管理服务器，用户可以安全地存储和管理他们的密码和敏感信息。对于 Yves 来说，这个项目可以帮助 Logic Labs 在开发与安全相关的 AI 应用时保障用户数据安全，同时也可以提升 TexTale 的电商平台安全性，增强用户的信任感。作为创意设计从业者，Yves 可以利用这个工具来保护设计资源和创意内容，确保其不被泄露。
